items.title: QQQ one bad day from a bear market: -10.5% in five sessions
items.idea: S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday to 6,910, breaking below the 7,100-7,400 'repricing zone' TMAD laid out in September. Over five sessions SPY fell 8.56% and QQQ 10.51%; QQQ closed almost 20% below its 52-week high. The author started buying Friday but kept most of the cash in reserve. The rest (bottom checklist on $MRVL $NVDA $MU $AVGO $META $AMZN) is paywalled.
items.angle: A 10% Nasdaq week with a hiking Fed is a different animal from the 2025 dips. The scale-in-but-hold-cash posture is what a 'first leg' looks like, not a capitulation.
items.tweetA: QQQ -10.5% in 5 sessions. That's not a correction pace, it's a deleveraging pace. And the Fed is still pencilled in to hike in 2 weeks. Bottoms usually need the Fed to blink first. $QQQ $SPY
items.tweetB: Everyone's asking 'is the bottom in?' Better question: who still has to sell? HFs already cut leverage to Liberation Day levels, but FMS cash is still near record lows. Retail is the last unhedged holder. $QQQ

items.title: Hartnett's Fed-put strike: S&P gives back ALL of 2026
items.idea: BofA's Michael Hartnett, after six straight weeks of 'reduce risk' calls, now puts a number on what it takes to sideline the Fed: equities must surrender their entire 2026 gain, alongside wider credit spreads. Only then does the tightening campaign get reconsidered.
items.angle: This is a precise, falsifiable Fed-put strike. If the S&P is already at 6,910, the distance to the 'Jan 1 level' is the market's remaining pain budget before policy relief.
items.tweetA: Hartnett's new Fed put strike: the S&P's Dec 31 close. Not a percentage, not a VIX level. Zero YTD. Which means the Fed is willing to let a full year of wealth effect evaporate before it flinches. $SPX
items.tweetB: The Fed hiking into a 10% Nasdaq week is the tell. In 2018 Powell folded at -20%. This Fed is explicitly anchoring on inflation, not equities. Hartnett's 'give back 2026' threshold may be the optimistic case.

items.title: Crash with no capitulation: FMS cash still near historic lows
items.idea: Per Hartnett, beneath last week's 'extraordinary liquidation', fund managers remain remarkably complacent: cash allocations sit near historic lows and investors keep pouring money into equities. The selloff has repriced assets without repricing positioning.
items.angle: Low cash after a ~9% drawdown means the dip-buying reflex is intact. That's bullish for a bounce but bearish for a durable low: nobody has surrendered yet.
items.tweetA: Price crashed. Positioning didn't. FMS cash near record lows after an 8.5% weekly S&P drop means the buyers of the dip are the same people who own the top. That's not a bottom, that's a pause.
items.tweetB: Contrarian take: low cash + falling prices is how bear markets extend, not end. The 2000-02 rallies all started with people 'buying the dip' from fully invested books. Watch for cash >5% before calling it.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Hartnett swaps the 2018 playbook for post-dot-com
items.idea: Hartnett argues the right analog isn't the Q4 2018 Fed-induced dip but the aftermath of the dot-com bubble, when spectacular relief rallies repeatedly convinced investors the worst was over before the adjustment resumed. AI capex and the equity wealth effect are now two pillars of US growth, so the virtuous loop can run in reverse.
items.angle: If AI capex and stock-market wealth are the growth engines, a drawdown is not just a P&L event, it's a GDP event. That reflexivity is what makes 2000-02 the right template.
items.tweetA: 2018 analog: Fed blinks, V-bottom, new highs in 4 months. 2000 analog: three 20% rallies inside a 49% decline. Hartnett is now picking door #2. The difference is whether AI capex is the economy or just in it.
items.tweetB: AI capex + equity wealth effect = two pillars of US growth. Pull one, the other wobbles. Capex gets cut when the stock punishes it; consumption drops when the portfolio does. The reflexive loop works both ways. $NVDA $META $AMZN

items.title: Goldman: HF VIP basket's worst relative stretch in 20 years
items.idea: Goldman Sachs prime data shows the most popular hedge fund positions have suffered one of their worst stretches of relative performance in two decades, exposing how dependent the market had become on the same crowded AI trades. The damage runs deeper than headline indices suggest.
items.angle: When the VIP basket breaks this hard, the unwind is mechanical (risk-manager driven), and the best shorts are the stocks HFs still can't exit. Crowding data becomes a trade signal in its own right.
items.tweetA: Worst 20-year stretch for the HF VIP basket. The 'smart money' wasn't diversified; it was one AI trade wearing 30 tickers. Index down 9%, crowded longs down a lot more.
items.tweetB: Hidden signal: when the VIP basket gets wrecked AND leverage is cut, the forced selling is mostly done. The next leg down needs new sellers. That's when crowding becomes a contrarian long list.

items.title: Leverage cut to Liberation Day levels, concentration untouched
items.idea: Hedge funds cut leverage to levels last seen around the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff, but per Goldman, lowering gross hasn't removed the concentration inside portfolios: books are smaller, not more diversified.
items.angle: Degrossing without de-concentrating means the same names remain the pressure points. Any second shock hits the same stocks again.
items.tweetA: HF leverage back at Liberation Day lows. But concentration hasn't moved. Smaller book, same bets. If the next shock comes, it hits the same 20 names twice.
items.tweetB: Liberation Day 2025 leverage lows marked a generational buy. Same leverage today, but this time the Fed is hiking, not about to cut. Same reading, very different macro.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Rotation, not retreat: funds broaden into cyclicals and defensives
items.idea: Beneath the tech liquidation, hedge funds are broadening exposure across both cyclical and defensive sectors rather than simply moving to cash, and the hierarchy of single-stock HF favourites is reshuffling as investors reassess where the next leg of equity performance comes from.
items.angle: Barbell rotation (cyclicals + defensives at once) is what a market does when it's unsure whether the problem is AI-specific or macro. Tracking which side wins tells you the regime.
items.tweetA: Funds aren't fleeing to cash. They're buying cyclicals AND defensives at the same time. That's a market that thinks AI is the problem, not the economy. If they're wrong, the defensives win. $XLI $XLP
items.tweetB: The new HF favourite list will be the tell for 2027. I'm watching whether energy and industrials enter the top-10 VIP names. That's when 'broadening' becomes the new crowded trade.

items.title: Against consensus: 2 Fed hikes in next 6 meetings, next one in ~2 weeks
items.idea: MacroEdge expects the Fed to hike again in a little over two weeks and pencils in 2 hikes over the next 6 FOMC meetings vs the 1 consensus now prices. Deflation is 'not a particularly high item on the list of risks' despite the equity drawdown and the louder 'deflationista' crowd.
items.angle: An energy desk calling for MORE hikes than consensus while equities crash is a useful counter-read to the 'Fed put' narrative. Front-end pricing is the cleanest expression.
items.tweetA: Equities down 9% in a week and an energy analyst is calling for 2 more hikes, not 1. If he's right, Hartnett's 'Fed put at 0% YTD' strike is too generous. The front end is the cheap trade here.
items.tweetB: Every drawdown brings the 'deflation is coming' crowd. But WTI is still in the $80s and the SPR is still being drained to keep it there. That's not a deflationary setup, that's suppressed inflation.

items.title: Oil will be first to sniff a Fed capitulation: WTI $90 'rather quickly'
items.idea: MacroEdge thinks oil will be one of the first commodities to price a Fed that goes weak-kneed. If the Fed softens or capitulates on its tighter regime, WTI could move back to $90/bbl quickly. $80-82 remains the key support level for the cycle.
items.angle: Oil as a long-dated Fed-pivot call option: downside protected by Hormuz/SPR dynamics at $80-82, upside convex to a dovish turn.
items.tweetA: Oil sold off on 'growth fears' while Hormuz flows tightened for two weeks. Fundamentals tighter, price lower. The day the Fed blinks, that gap closes violently. $80-82 floor, $90 target. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Trade structure: WTI is the cheapest Fed-pivot option on the board. If the Fed holds, you've got Hormuz and SPR depletion as the floor. If it folds, you've got $90. Asymmetry is the point.

items.title: Iran about to run its own ships through Hormuz to break the blockade
items.idea: Iran is now very close to moving its own ships through the Strait of Hormuz to break the blockade, which MacroEdge thinks the Trump administration will 'sort of... let it do' despite tough sanctions talk. Iran has about one month of economic runway before it is forced to escalate, and is poking the bear with relatively minor exchanges of blows over the past few days.
items.angle: A one-month Iranian economic clock creates a dated catalyst for oil volatility into late December. Ghost-tanker tracking and freight rates become the leading indicators.
items.tweetA: Iran has ~1 month of economic runway before it has to escalate. That's a dated catalyst into Christmas, and oil vol isn't pricing a calendar. Watch tanker rates before you watch Brent.
items.tweetB: The quiet outcome nobody prices: Washington lets Iranian ships through, talks tough, and the 'blockade' becomes a toll booth. That's more Iranian barrels, lower crude, and a big win for ghost-fleet freight. $FRO $DHT

items.title: Oil 'only' in low $80s because of unprecedented coordination and SPR draining
items.idea: MacroEdge: people find it hard to believe WTI is only in the low-to-mid $80s, but the cycle has seen coordination and intervention 'to a degree we haven't seen in any previous cycle.' The US is still drawing down the SPR and will be 'for some time.' Late-cycle loud money hasn't really shown up in energy at all, which is a positive.
items.angle: Policy-suppressed prices with no speculative froth = coiled spring. The SPR draw is a finite resource, so its end date is a supply event.
items.tweetA: WTI in the low $80s isn't the market price. It's the market price minus the SPR. Every barrel pulled out now is a barrel that has to be bought back later. That's a deferred bid, not a lower price.
items.tweetB: Strange energy setup: Hormuz disrupted, SPR draining, and yet the tourists never showed up. No retail froth, no crowded long. Lowest-sentiment supply shock I've seen.

items.title: Friday's tell: liquids became the safe haven, royalty names lead
items.idea: On Friday, liquids became the safe haven while natgas tightened on its fundamental outlook, offering a 'genuine glimmer' that energy may decouple from the everything-to-correlation-1 growth-fear trade. Royalty and non-op names have outperformed the broader energy basket. The note also flags record-high Henry Hub production that 'doesn't mean there aren't opportunities.'
items.angle: Royalty/non-op outperformance is the low-capex, cash-yield end of energy, which is exactly where you'd hide in a hiking cycle with high oil.
items.tweetA: On the worst Nasdaq day of the year, oil acted like a safe haven. Correlation-1 regimes break first in the asset with real-world scarcity. $XLE
items.tweetB: Royalty names outperforming the energy basket is the market saying: I want oil exposure without capex risk. In a hiking cycle that's the cleanest version. $TPL $VNOM $KRP

items.title: GTA VI: 5,000 humans, no gen-AI, $3.79B on day one
items.idea: Rockstar's 5,000 staff built Grand Theft Auto VI without generative AI; reportedly 30,000 unique characters were made by hand. It made $3.79B in sales by the end of day one (incl. preorders). Azhar revives his 2017 'artisanal cheesemaker' thesis: when AI makes perfection cheap, human imperfection becomes scarce. In one study people rated AI paintings more favorably when labeled human-made.
items.angle: 'Certified human' may become a premium tier in content, with labeling/provenance (C2PA, watermarking) as the infrastructure. $TTWO is a live test case.
items.tweetA: GTA VI did $3.79B on day one with 5,000 people and zero gen-AI. That's ~$760K of revenue per employee in 24 hours. 'Made by humans' just became a pricing strategy. $TTWO
items.tweetB: Same painting, rated higher when labeled 'human.' That's not an art finding, it's a market structure finding: provenance is about to be monetized. Whoever owns the 'certified human' label owns a toll road.

items.title: The William Morris trap: does 'handmade' end up as a luxury for the rich?
items.idea: Morris and the 19th-century Arts and Crafts movement resisted mechanization only to find hand labor couldn't compete on price; Morris raged he spent his life 'ministering to the swinish luxury of the rich.' Azhar argues digital culture might escape the trap because a hand-made product's cost is spread across millions of buyers, but an ocean of synthetic content could still drown out a scarcer 'certified human' tier.
items.angle: The key variable is marginal cost: physical handmade stays elite, digital handmade can be mass-market. That splits winners: IP-owning studios vs. physical crafts.
items.tweetA: William Morris lost because handmade couldn't scale. GTA VI wins because handmade digital scales to 100M buyers at zero marginal cost. The artisanal premium only survives where copying is free.
items.tweetB: The Morris problem in 2026: if AI drivel floods every feed, the 'human' tier doesn't disappear, it gets discovered less. Distribution, not production, becomes the scarce asset.

items.title: What did Wall Street actually buy in the Anthropic IPO?
items.idea: EV frames the Anthropic listing as a bet on whether Anthropic can take a cut of the value its AI creates across the intangible economy, and models three futures: from licensing models that run on your devices to becoming an AI utility. Jasmine Sun's year of conversations with insiders finds the firm has 'hallmarks of a religion': race to build the dangerous tech first because only they are virtuous enough to wield it.
items.angle: The three-scenario frame (device licensing vs. utility) is a good way to bracket the valuation range of $ANT post-IPO volatility.
items.tweetA: Is Anthropic a software company, a utility, or a royalty on the intangible economy? Those are three different multiples. The 22% day-two drop is the market not knowing which one it bought.
items.tweetB: 'Hallmarks of a religion' is a feature for retention, a bug for governance. The most valuable IPO asset might be a workforce that believes it's saving the world. Hard to poach a believer.

items.title: Two Riemann hypothesis proofs in one day: Claude+Lean vs 'all human'
items.idea: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he and Claude may have proved the Riemann hypothesis, in 17.4M lines of Lean. The same day, Stanford's Ravi Vakil rushed out Alessandro Masullo's 'all human, no AI' proof, now being translated into Lean for faster verification. Scott Aaronson notes no Lean-verified AI result has ever been retracted.
items.angle: Formal verification is becoming the arbiter of truth even for human proofs. The bottleneck in math is shifting from discovery to verification compute.
items.tweetA: 17.4 million lines of Lean. No human will ever read that proof. We just moved mathematical trust from the referee to the compiler, and the humans are now racing to get their proof into Lean too.
items.tweetB: The tell isn't that AI may have proved Riemann. It's that the human team immediately reached for Lean to defend theirs. Formal verification just became the peer review standard for everyone.

items.title: 2,000+ GW in the US interconnection queue — more than the entire grid
items.idea: More than 2,000 GW of new plants and batteries are waiting to connect to the US grid, more than every power plant currently running. About 85% is solar, wind and storage. Solar modules keep getting 24% cheaper with every doubling of capacity (Wright's law).
items.angle: The queue is the binding constraint, not generation economics. Anything that lets you skip the queue (behind-the-meter, transmission, interconnect engineering) has pricing power.
items.tweetA: The US interconnection queue (2,000 GW) is bigger than the US grid (~1,300 GW). We're not short of power. We're short of permission to plug it in. $PWR $ETN
items.tweetB: Wright's law keeps cutting solar 24% per doubling; the interconnection process doesn't follow any learning curve at all. Physics got cheap, paperwork didn't. That spread is the trade.

charts.desc: 1 chart — interconnection queue by technology vs installed capacity. 🔥 Queue > entire fleet is a one-image story

items.title: A month waiting for power costs more than the power: AI goes off-grid
items.idea: An AI chip rents for about $3/hour, so a month spent waiting for a grid connection costs more than the electricity itself. EV's Investment Brief found on-site solar plus batteries is now the cheapest option to power data centers in half of the United States: 'the queue is pushing AI off the grid.'
items.angle: Behind-the-meter solar+storage for DCs is a direct beneficiary of queue backlog. Watch $FSLR, $ENPH-adjacent storage, $TSLA energy, and gas-turbine competitors.
items.tweetA: The math: $3/hr GPU × 720 hrs = ~$2,160/month. The power for that GPU is maybe $80. A 1-month grid delay costs ~27x the electricity bill. That's why data centers are building their own grids. $FSLR $TSLA
items.tweetB: Utilities thought AI demand was their growth story. Instead, the interconnection queue is teaching hyperscalers to leave. Behind-the-meter solar+batteries cheapest in half the US. Rate-base growth just got a competitor.

charts.desc: 1 chart — LCOE map of on-site solar+storage vs grid for data centers

items.title: From checks to taxes to ownership: every AI wealth-sharing plan on the table
items.idea: Parekh maps the convergence: Altman's 2021 American Equity Fund; Altman 2026 favoring collective ownership (compute/equity stakes) over UBI; OpenAI's 'Public Wealth Fund' + shifting taxes from labor to capital + subsidized 4-day week; talks on a 5% US govt stake in OpenAI (~$320/household at $852B); Amodei's call for basic income funded by AI taxes + Anthropic's $200M Economic Futures fund; a House bill taxing 2% of token value or 3% of AI revenue, rising automatically with unemployment; Sanders' 50% public stake.
items.angle: A token tax indexed to unemployment is an automatic stabilizer that hits AI margins exactly when the narrative is weakest. That's a new tail risk for AI equity multiples.
items.tweetA: The House AI bill taxes 2% of token value and RISES automatically as unemployment rises. That's a margin hit that triggers in a recession. An AI multiple with a built-in countercyclical tax is not the same multiple. $ANT $NVDA
items.tweetB: 5% govt stake in OpenAI was ~$320/household at $852B in July. At the $1.25T IPO target it's ~$470. The 'public wealth fund' idea gets more popular every time the valuation goes up. Politics follows the cap table.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: ~$500B of demand for a ~5% float, 20% reserved for retail
items.idea: Anthropic planned to set aside up to 20% of IPO shares for individuals. Retail indications approached $100B next to ~$400B from institutions, more demand than SpaceX saw for its $85.7B June offering. But the float was only ~5% of a company valued at well over $1T; insiders keep most of the upside.
items.angle: A tiny float with massive non-binding demand is a classic setup for day-one pop then sharp fade as indications don't convert. Lock-up expiry dates are the next catalyst.
items.tweetA: $500B of IPO demand for a ~$70B float — roughly 7x oversubscribed. Then the stock fell ~22% on day two. Non-binding demand is the most bullish fiction in markets. $ANT
items.tweetB: Retail asked for ~$100B of Anthropic. Institutions $400B. With ~95% still held by insiders, the real IPO is the lock-up expiry. Mark that date.

items.title: Agent gatekeeping has begun: Amazon blocked Meta's #1 agent app
items.idea: Meta's Muse agent app hit #1 on the US App Store in September and Amazon promptly blocked it from shopping on Amazon. Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) and commerce standards are early rails for agents spending on our behalf. Parekh: 'who owns the agents?' is already a live business fight, not a 2040 question.
items.angle: Agent access to marketplaces is the new app-store/antitrust front. Payment rails for agents (AP2, Visa/Mastercard agent tokens, stablecoins) are where value accrues.
items.tweetA: Amazon blocking Meta's agent from shopping is the first shot of the agent wars. Whoever controls which agents can transact controls the next decade of e-commerce take rates. $AMZN $META $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Agents need to pay. Cards weren't built for a bot that buys 400 times a day. Google's AP2, card-network agent tokens, and stablecoins are all fighting for the same rail. That's the quiet infra trade. $V $MA

items.title: Gradual disempowerment: AI could turn every state into a petrostate
items.idea: The 'Gradual Disempowerment' authors borrow the rentier-state idea: governments funded by oil, not taxes, answer less to citizens. If states and companies no longer need human work, the incentive to keep humans happy weakens, 'no takeover required.' Ruxandra Teslo: work is leverage, and UBI doesn't explain how people would come to own capital.
items.angle: The petrostate analogy is a useful political-economy lens: AI-rent states could look like Gulf states (generous transfers, low voice) or Norway (sovereign fund).
items.tweetA: Oil-funded states don't need citizens' taxes, so they don't need citizens' consent. Now swap 'oil' for 'AI compute.' The real AI risk might not be Skynet. It's Saudi Arabia for everyone.
items.tweetB: Norway vs Venezuela is the real AI policy fork. Same resource curse; one built a sovereign fund, one didn't. The US 'public wealth fund' debate is just the Norway option arriving early.

items.title: AI optimism map: Nigeria, Vietnam, India, Brazil far more bullish than US/Europe
items.idea: Global polls last month showed people in Nigeria, Vietnam, India and Brazil far more optimistic about AI than Americans or Europeans. Parekh: for most of the eight billion, AI looks like a ladder up, not a handout. He still expects tech waves to create more work than they destroy, over decades not quarters.
items.angle: Adoption follows optimism: EM consumer AI adoption could outpace DM, favoring local distribution platforms and cheap open models.
items.tweetA: The countries most optimistic about AI are the ones with the least to lose from it. Nigeria, Vietnam, India: AI as a ladder. US/Europe: AI as a threat to incumbency. Adoption curves will follow that map.
items.tweetB: If the West regulates AI out of fear and the Global South adopts it out of hope, the next wave of AI users is in Lagos and Ho Chi Minh City. Cheap open models win that market, not $200/month subscriptions.

items.title: Anthropic: $1.5T IPO, $1.175T next day — 14th most valuable company
items.idea: Anthropic IPO'd Thursday at a $1.5T valuation, second only to SpaceX's $1.77T. By the next day it had fallen to $1.175T, the 14th most valuable company in the world. Noah Smith bought on day one and remains very bullish: he sees a talent-hedged, cross-domain conglomerate in the mould of Google in 2004, and would more than double if it reaches Google/Microsoft-scale value.
items.angle: A ~22% day-two drop on a tiny float, during a 10% Nasdaq week, is mostly macro. OpenAI's $1.25T IPO target now sits above where Anthropic trades.
items.tweetA: Anthropic: -22% on day two. ~$325B of market cap gone in 24 hours, bigger than almost any single S&P 500 company. During a week QQQ dropped 10.5%. Worst possible tape for the biggest AI IPO ever. $ANT
items.tweetB: OpenAI is targeting a $1.25T IPO. Anthropic now trades at $1.175T. Either OpenAI cuts its price, or the market decides OpenAI is worth more than the company growing faster. Watch that spread.

items.title: 5,300 employees, $331B pool, more centimillionaires than Los Angeles
items.idea: Andrew Benson's breakdown at a $2T valuation: $199B for 7 co-founders (~10%), $100B for the Public Benefit Fund, $331B in employee options/RSUs for ~5,300 staff (avg $62M). ~940 people hired by end-2024 average nine figures. That would mean more centimillionaires than LA; even at 350-400 it matches Houston+Dallas+Austin. Founders+employees hold as much wealth as the bottom third of Americans combined.
items.angle: Lock-up expiry for thousands of newly wealthy employees = SF luxury real estate, angel/VC formation, and a potential supply overhang on $ANT.
items.tweetA: At today's ~$1.2T, Anthropic's employee pool is still ~$200B. That's ~$37M per employee. When lockups end, that's the biggest new angel investor class in history hitting Silicon Valley at once.
items.tweetB: 5,300 people hold roughly as much wealth as the bottom third of Americans, ~110M people. That's not a startup outcome, it's a political event. Expect AI wealth taxes to be a 2028 campaign plank.

items.title: 'Post-economic at 22': AI wealth is warping a generation's idea of work
items.idea: Sarah Chieng: build a startup in 9 months, get acqui-hired by OpenAI, Anthropic or Cognition, and walk away a multimillionaire; join the right company at 22 and become 'effectively post-economic.' Noah notes former potluck friends now host parties in designer mansions on SF hilltops; some are under-30 billionaires. He asks what happens to elite tensions if only the AI class gets rich going forward.
items.angle: Second-order effects: talent drain from every other sector (finance, academia, government), SF housing pressure, and a new political class of young AI wealth.
items.tweetA: When 22-year-olds become 'post-economic', the cost isn't inequality, it's talent allocation. Every smart person who'd have become a doctor, regulator, or scientist now targets one of three companies.
items.tweetB: Noah asks what happens if only AI people get rich. History answer: the Gilded Age. Railroads created wealth, then trustbusting, then an income tax. The AI version of the 16th Amendment is already being drafted.
